title: What N4 Means for Japanese Learners, Updated Nov 2026
summary: What JLPT N4 really means for Japanese learners, plus the five gaps keeping you stuck before N3. November 2026 guide.
body_markdown:
Reaching JLPT N4 means you can read everyday hiragana and katakana, recognize about 300 kanji, and follow slow speech on familiar topics. What you probably can't do yet is answer a native speaker at normal pace without stalling on a te-form or defaulting to the same five verbs. That's a specific gap, not a vague intermediate slump, and it closes with specific changes to how you practice. Here's what N4 actually looks like in speech and what moves you toward N3.


**TLDR:**


- JLPT N4 means roughly 300 kanji, 1,500 vocabulary items, and slow conversation on familiar topics, mapping to upper A2 on CEFR
- The N4-to-N3 plateau comes from five compounding gaps: listening at native speed, keigo avoidance, overreliance on 20-30 verbs, particle fossilization, and read-but-can't-speak freeze
- Swain's Output Hypothesis (1985) explains why daily spoken reps beat rereading: production under pressure forces you to notice gaps input-only study hides
- FSI classifies Japanese as Category IV requiring ~2,200 hours; N4 to N3 typically takes another 350-500 hours depending on weekly commitment
- ISSEN's AI voice tutor supplies unlimited conversational reps with turn-by-turn pacing and keigo register switching, with pronunciation drilling handled separately in Shadowing mode


## Introduction


If you have just passed the JLPT N4, or you have been studying long enough to feel like you sit around that level, you are in a specific and frustrating spot. Japanese N4 is the upper-elementary stage: you can read everyday text in hiragana and katakana, follow slow conversation on familiar topics, and recognize roughly 300 kanji. What you cannot yet do is follow Japanese at native speed or hold a spontaneous conversation about anything abstract without stalling.


This article covers what N4 learners can say out loud, where almost everyone plateaus between N4 and N3, and the changes in speaking practice that close the gap.


## What JLPT N4 actually means


N4 is the second rung of the JLPT, and the official framework describes it as the ability to understand basic Japanese used in everyday situations when speech is slow and vocabulary familiar ([JLPT level summary](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/about/levelsummary.html) ). You can read short passages in hiragana, katakana, and about 300 common kanji, follow slow daily conversation, order food, and describe your job in plain sentences. N4 roughly maps to upper[Japanese A2](https://www.issen.com/blog/japanese-a2-jlpt-n5-what-you-can-say/) on the CEFR scale.


### A short N4 exchange


週末は何をしましたか。 友達と映画を見ました。あまり面白くなかったです。


(What did you do over the weekend? I saw a movie with a friend. It wasn't very interesting.)


Representative N4 output: past tense, i-adjective negation, familiar topic.


## The JLPT N4 skill checklist


Use this checklist to gauge where you actually sit. If you can tick seven or more without hedging, you are solidly at N4; if several feel shaky, you have more N4 consolidation to do before N3 becomes realistic.


- Read around 300 kanji in context, including compounds like 時間, 電車, and 会社
- Hold roughly 1,500 vocabulary items in active or recognizable memory
- Conjugate verbs into て-form, た-form, ない-form, and swap between plain and polite (〜ます) registers without stopping to think
- Follow slow, clearly enunciated Japanese on familiar topics
- Describe your daily routine using 〜ています (毎朝コーヒーを飲んでいます)
- Give simple reasons with から and ので (疲れたから、早く寝ます)
- Read short graded readers, or try[learning Japanese through anime and manga](https://www.issen.com/blog/best-way-learn-japanese-anime-manga/) , with occasional dictionary lookups
- Write a few paragraphs about yourself, your job, or your weekend
- Freeze when keigo (尊敬語, 謙譲語) is expected in work or service situations
- Lose the thread when native speakers talk at normal pace or drop particles


## Typical vocabulary range at JLPT N4


N4 vocabulary sits at roughly 1,500 active words and about 300 kanji, cumulative with N5, per the official[JLPT level summary](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/about/levelsummary.html) published by the Japan Foundation and Japan Educational Exchanges and Services. Growth happens in three categories: time expressions, daily-routine verbs, and feeling adjectives. These are the words you reach for when a Japanese speaker asks about your week.


A dozen entries you should have close to automatic:


- 用意する (youi suru): to prepare. Used for meals, meetings, trips.
- 急ぐ (isogu): to hurry. Pairs with 間に合う.
- 必要 (hitsuyou): necessary. Often 必要です or 必要な〜.
- 違う (chigau): to differ, to be wrong.
- 間に合う (ma ni au): to be on time.
- 心配 (shinpai): worry. 心配しないで is a daily phrase.
- 都合 (tsugou): schedule. 都合がいい = works for me.
- それで (sorede): and so. Links two clauses.
- 〜なければなりません: must do. Obligation structure.
- 〜てもいいです: may do. Permission grammar.
- 〜たことがあります: have done before. Opens experience talk.


## Grammar you should have locked in


Most N4 textbooks introduce these as reading targets. Producing them under conversational pressure, without a two-second pause to assemble the verb stem, is what N3 actually demands.


- て-form chaining (〜て、〜ます): link actions in sequence. 朝起きて、ご飯を食べて、学校に行きます。
- Potential form (〜られる/〜える): express ability. 漢字が読めます。
- Plain-form conjugation: shift register with friends or inside embedded clauses. 明日来る？
- 〜なければならない: obligation. 明日までに書かなければなりません。
- 〜たり〜たりする: list representative actions. 週末は本を読んだり、散歩したりします。
- 〜と思います: give an opinion. この映画は面白いと思います。
- Conditional 〜たら: if/when a condition is met. 時間があったら、電話します。


Pulling the right one out mid-sentence, with the correct conjugation, is the skill N3 assumes you already have.


## Where JLPT N4 learners get stuck


The plateau between N4 and N3 is five problems that compound.


### Listening collapses at native speed


Textbook audio enunciates every syllable. Real speech reduces 〜ている to 〜てる, swallows 〜ておく into 〜とく, and drops を in casual registers.


### Keigo avoidance


Most N4 learners cling to です・ます and never build 尊敬語 or 謙譲語 into active production. You can chat with a friend but freeze when a client expects お〜になる.


### Overreliance on 20-30 verbs


する, ある, 行く, 見る and a handful of others carry most of your output. Verbs like 伝える, 済ませる, 気づく sit in passive memory because you have never retrieved them under time pressure.


### Particle fossilization


は/が and に/で mistakes become habitual when nobody corrects them in the moment. Conversation demands the right particle in 200 milliseconds, and wrong choices get reinforced every time they go unflagged.


### The read-but-can't-speak freeze


You can recognize the grammar on a page while still freezing when you try to produce it out loud. Swain's Output Hypothesis explains the mechanism, a principle at the core of[how AI speaking practice works](https://www.issen.com/blog/how-ai-speaking-practice-works/) : producing language under conversational pressure forces learners to notice gaps that input-only study hides ([Swain, 1985](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1095572.pdf) ).

## Sample conversation at JLPT N4


Here is a short exchange with an ISSEN tutor named Yuki. The learner sits at N4, and Yuki nudges toward N3 without breaking the flow.


**Yuki:** 週末はどこかに行きましたか。 **Learner:** はい、箱根に行きました。温泉に入ったり、山を見たりしました。 **Yuki:** いいですね。前にも行ったことがありますか。¹ **Learner:** いいえ、初めてでした。電車が混んでいたから、疲れました。 **Yuki:** 混雑していると大変ですよね。² 温泉はどうでしたか。 **Learner:** とても気持ちよかったです。また行きたいです。 **Yuki:** ぜひ。次は紅葉の季節に行ってみてはいかがですか。³


(Yuki: Did you go anywhere this weekend? Learner: Yes, I went to Hakone, soaked in the hot springs, and looked at the mountains. Yuki: Nice. Have you been before? Learner: No, first time. The train was crowded, so I got tired. Yuki: That is rough when the train gets packed. How were the hot springs? Learner: Really good. I want to go again. Yuki: How about the autumn leaves season next time?)


**Notes**


1. 〜たことがありますか invites past-experience talk, a core N4 structure.
2. 混雑している is a slight N3 upgrade from 混んでいる, modeled in context.
3. 〜てみてはいかがですか is softer N3 phrasing for polite suggestions.


## How long to reach JLPT N3


Timelines from N4 to N3 vary by learner, though[how long it takes to learn Japanese](https://www.issen.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-learn-japanese/) overall depends on similar institutional baselines. The FSI classifies Japanese as a Category IV language needing roughly[2,200 classroom hours](https://www.state.gov/foreign-language-training/) for professional proficiency. Reaching N4 is a separate, earlier milestone within that total; the N4-to-N3 gap itself typically takes another 350 to 500 hours on top of whatever got you to N4.

## FAQ


### Am I really at N4 or lower?


If you can read short daily-topic passages, handle slow conversation on familiar topics, and recognize around 300 kanji, you are likely at N4. If past-tense conjugation still trips you up, you are closer to N5.


### How do I test my N4 level?


Start with the official JLPT N4 sample questions on jlpt.jp, then try a timed third-party mock. Clearing reading and listening inside the official time limit is the clearest signal you are at level.


### Can I skip straight to N3?


N3 assumes N4 grammar is automatic, not merely recognizable. Skipping N4 output practice usually means freezing on て-form chains halfway through a sentence.


### Is N4 enough for work in Japan?


Most Japanese workplaces expect N2 or N3 plus working keigo, so N4 alone will not carry you through professional contexts.


### What's the fastest way off the N4 plateau?


Shift to daily spoken output. 15 to 20 minutes a day producing N4 grammar under time pressure moves the needle faster than any amount of rereading.


## Conclusion


N4 is a real, defined stage with clear markers. You can read short passages, hold slow conversation, and recognize around 300 kanji. N3 is reachable, though stacking more vocabulary apps on what you already recognize will not get you there. The gap closes with daily spoken reps and real-time feedback, where retrieval happens under pressure and hidden gaps finally surface.
